newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Cholera epidemic kills 12 in Orinoco Delta.
newsitem.headline: Cholera epidemic kills 12 in Orinoco Delta.

text.p: The death toll from a cholera epidemic in Venezuela's Orinoco delta has risen to 12 since January, but the number of new cases were falling fast, according to the region's director of health Gladys de Suarez.

New cases reached a peak in April when doctors started an intensive diagnosis and treatment plan, and 275 people have now been infected by the disease, she said in an interview in the remote state capital Tucupita on Friday.
It was the second such outbreak within five years, reflecting the chronic health problems and lack of medical resources in Venezuela's poorest region.

Diarrhoea, tuberculosis, malaria, malnutrition and high infant mortality were the most serious problems for the delta, which numbers 25,000 indigenous Warao Indians among its 120,000 inhabitants, she said.

The current cholera epidemic was concentrated in the Warao community, who carried it from the remote Mariusa island inland to the market town of Barrancas de Orinoco and then out to other Indian settlements in the delta.
New cases were now restricted to Curiapo, the capital of Antonio Diaz municipality located deep in the delta.

In a region covering 16,000 square miles (42,000 square kilometres) of swampy forest and river channels, 60 percent of which is water, Suarez said the government had between nine and 18 rural doctors and not a single boat.
"This is a serious limitation ... but we are hoping to receive three boats next week," she said.
Many of the biggest killers in the region were easily preventible and were linked to the lack of drinking water, sanitation and education.
"In rural areas, all the inhabitants of the river edge drink water from the river and all the waste, including solid waste, goes straight into the river without any treatment at all," Suarez said.
